header: Date: 2026-11-12 | Time: 15:00 PT | Duration: 62 mins | Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Laguna Head of Security), Anita Bose (Laguna Cloud Architect), Tom Hayes (Compliance), Priya Nair (Network)
summary: Deep technical review of Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) security architecture focusing on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, RBAC/SSO, audit logs, and encryption/KMS options. Customer requested details on data residency, audit retention, and customer-managed key options. Action items include sharing compliance artifacts, providing VPC diagrams, and scheduling a pilot for egress testing.
topics: VPC network isolation, ingress/egress and firewall rules
On-prem deployment considerations and egress whitelisting
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we're pretty excited to walk through the Private VPC security architecture. I'm Jordan, AE for Redwood, and with me is Maya Chen, our solutions engineer. 
[00:12] Carlos: Hi Jordan, hi Maya, Carlos Ruiz here. We've got a few folks from Laguna security and cloud. Appreciate you taking the time.
[00:20] Anita: Anita Bose, cloud architect. Quick note we are evaluating private/on-prem because of strict data residency and our audit requirements.
[00:30] Jordan: Totally understood. quick agenda: compliance artifacts, auth/identity, key management and encryption, logging/audit, network — ingress/egress, firewalls, and then open Q&A. Sound good?
[00:40] Tom: Works for me. We have SOC 2 and ISO requirements, expecting evidence and also runbook-level details.
[02:05] Maya: Ok starting on the compliance side — Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001 attestation; we have a redwood security deck and we can share the pen test summary. For Private deployments we support a customer-managed control plane or a private control plane behind your VPC, so you keep the network boundary. Link to deck: https://redwood.ai/security-deck (shared).
[04:10] Carlos: When you say private control plane behind our VPC, do you mean the control plane sits in our account and we manage KMS and VPC peering? or is it a hosted managed control plane? 
[04:30] Maya: Good question — we have two patterns. 1) Private VPC: Redwood control plane runs in Redwood infra but is connected via private endpoints and peering — traffic to the inference nodes is routed entirely within your VPC via VPC peering or PrivateLink; KMS can be customer-managed (AWS KMS CMKs) so you bring keys. 2) On-prem / air-gapped: we ship an on-prem package where you run the control plane and inference runtime in your environment; in that case keys, network egress, everything stays in your environment.
[07:20] Anita: For Laguna we are leaning toward a managed private VPC inside our cloud account with customer managed KMS. What does key rotation and HSM integration look like?
[07:40] Maya: We support AWS KMS and can integrate with external HSMs using PKCS#11 where necessary — there is a recommended flow: encryption at rest for model artifacts and disk using CMK, TLS for in-flight; application-level envelope encryption for sensitive prompt payloads is also supported. Rotation: you can rotate CMKs as you normally would; we recommend staged rotation with versioned secrets in our runtime config.
[10:00] Carlos: Is there any plaintext sensitive data that ever leaves the VPC or hits Redwood-managed storage?
[10:15] Jordan: For Private VPC, by default nothing leaves the VPC to Redwood-managed storage. Unless you opt-in to cross-account backups, which would be documented and encrypted with your keys. For hosted mode obviously data flows to Redwood tenancy.
[12:05] Tom: Audit logs — we need 7 years of immutable audit logs for a subset of control plane activities. Does Redwood push logs to our S3 and do they support WORM / Object Lock?
[12:30] Maya: Yes, logs can be shipped to your S3 bucket via our log exporter. We can sign logs with object lock if your S3 supports it. We also provide a streaming option to your SIEM via Kinesis or Eventbridge; log schema includes request_id, user_id (SAML subject), model_version, route, and ingress IP.
[15:00] Priya: For networking, what does ingress look like — do you require public IPs on inference nodes?
[15:20] Maya: No public IPs required. We can front the runtime with private NLBs or PrivateLink endpoints. Inference nodes live in private subnets. Ingress is via customer-controlled NAT or a private endpoint; for API access from your app-plane you can use VPC peering or transit gateway.
[17:40] Anita: How do you handle egress — like pull model for model updates or telemetry? We have strict egress filtering.
[18:00] Maya: Good point. For private VPC we operate in a pull model only when allowed — image/model updates can be pulled from your artifact repo or from a signed Redwood repository but using customer-managed endpoints. If you block all outbound, we support manual offline updates (you feed model tarballs). For telemetry, telemetry is optional; we can keep all metrics internal to the VPC and stream to your monitoring endpoints.
[20:30] Priya: We run an enterprise firewall (Palo Alto) and have an egress proxy; we'll need a list of domains/IP ranges to whitelist if using managed pulls.
[20:45] Maya: We'll provide a CIDR/IP list and fully qualified domain names. We also support using your proxy: the runtime can be configured to go via customer HTTP proxy with mTLS to the update endpoints.
[23:10] Carlos: On firewalling, do you have guidance for security groups vs NACLs vs appliance-level rules?
[23:30] Maya: Recommendation: network segmentation using multiple private subnets: inference (GPU) subnets, control plane subnets, admin subnets. Security groups for east-west control (instance level), NACLs for subnet boundaries, and firewall appliance for egress filtering and IDS/IPS. Keep management plane behind a bastion host or session manager.
[25:00] Tom: For RBAC and SSO — we use Okta, SCIM for user provisioning, and SAML for SSO. We need per-route RBAC and auditability.
[25:20] Maya: We support SAML 2.0 for authentication and SCIM for user/group sync. RBAC is role-based at the API key/token level and also at route/model level: you can define roles that allow only embeddings, or only non-sensitive model routes. All actions are logged and include the SAML subject to map to your users.
[28:10] Anita: How granular can logging be? We need full request/response logging for a specific regulated workflow, but cannot store PII. Can you redact at capture-time?
[28:35] Maya: Yes, we have configurable log redaction rules — at capture time you can instruct the runtime to redact specific JSON fields or mask tokens. For extra protection we recommend client-side redaction or encrypting the payloads with your keys before sending if the content is extremely sensitive.
[32:00] Priya: What about IDS/monitoring and alerts for anomalous egress or model behavior?
[32:20] Maya: We provide hooks to your monitoring stack — CloudWatch, Datadog, Splunk via forwarders. We emit telemetry like unusual request patterns, spike in token volume, and failed auth events. You can also integrate with our tracing to see request lifecycles. For more advanced controls, put an IDS between subnets for east-west and monitor with flow logs.
[35:15] Carlos: Data residency — we need guarantees that training data or customer prompts are never used outside the tenant.
[35:40] Jordan: For Private/on-prem, customer data does not leave your environment unless explicitly configured. For hosted models we have data handling policies but you asked specifically about Private so yes, tenancy isolation is enforced and model cache is local to the deployment.
[38:50] Anita: Are there regulatory certifications for the on-prem pattern? We need artifact-level evidence for ISO and SOC2 in our vendor risk assessment.
[39:10] Jordan: We can provide SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 attestations for Redwood operations; for on-prem installations we provide a deployment checklist and runbook, as well as recommended config baselines that auditors accept. We also provide a signed statement about responsibilities (shared responsibility matrix).
[41:30] Tom: Pen testing — do you allow customer pen tests against the deployment?
[41:40] Maya: Yes, we allow coordinated pen tests. For managed Private in your account, you can run tests with notice and we'll provide a contact and scope confirmation. For on-prem we coordinate schedules.
[44:00] Priya: A practical question: can we restrict egress so only our artifact repo and NTP and a few telemetry endpoints are allowed? We want zero outbound except whitelisted.
[44:20] Maya: Absolutely. The runtime works in a zero-egress-by-default model for on-prem. For Private VPC, you can set strict security groups and NACLs and only allow specific egress IPs/domains. If you need model pulls, use your artifact repo or an S3 bucket with VPC endpoint.
[46:35] Carlos: How do you handle KV cache and model state — is any KV persisted outside the VM?
[46:50] Maya: KV cache is local to the inference node memory or local disk; persistence options are to your managed storage. By default, no KV is sent off-network. There's sometimes confusion since other docs say K-V cache but we keep it local.
[49:10] Anita: Any performance trade-offs we should be aware of when enabling strict egress and proxying updates?
[49:30] Maya: Proxying or forcing everything through an inspection appliance can add latency for model pulls and possibly for initial cold starts if you restrict bandwidth. For runtime inference traffic we recommend keeping the path internal to reduce added hop latency; model downloads can be scheduled off hours or via sidecar with dedicated throughput.
[52:00] Jordan: Quick note on fallback and high availability — we support multi-AZ placement within your VPC and can add failover nodes in another region if needed; cross-region introduces data residency constraints so that would be an explicit opt-in.
[54:20] Tom: For audit retention, we might need logs stored in immutable archives for 7 years and tamper evidence. You mentioned S3 object lock, can Redwood sign or attest logs?
[54:40] Maya: We can push logs to your S3 and include signatures; we also provide a digest and chain of custody metadata if you require.
[56:00] Carlos: Ok, sounds promising. A couple of remaining asks: a full VPC diagram with subnets, security groups, and firewall rules; a minimal whitelist for model updates and telemetry; SOC2/ISO docs and pen test summary.
[56:20] Jordan: We'll get those over. Maya will own the diagram and Priya will review the whitelist.
[58:05] Anita: One last question — does Redwood support customer HSM for signing model artifacts? We need HSM signing for certain artifacts.
[58:30] Maya: Yes — we can integrate with customer HSMs via PKCS#11 for signing workflows, or you can sign artifacts locally and we verify signatures as part of the deployment.
[60:00] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone. We'll recap the next steps and action items in an email and attach the security bundle. Thanks for your time.
[61:30] Tom: Thanks, talk soon.
[61:40] (meeting closed)
